data.title: Šimúnky, Hradište and Koscelisko – possible links in the Mariková valley
data.excerpt: Archaeologist Peter Schreiber wrote this study for our site on the possible course of ancient routes in Mariková and its surroundings. Working from place names, relief and the few known finds, he asks how the sites of Hradište, Koscelisko, Kňažová and Jazerka might be connected with the early medieval occupation at Šimúnky.
data.metaTitle: Šimúnky, Hradište and Koscelisko – possible links
data.metaDescription: Archaeologist Peter Schreiber on the possible course of ancient routes in Mariková and the links between the sites of Šimúnky, Hradište and Koscelisko.

children.text: Archaeologist
Peter Schreiber

wrote the following, exceptionally interesting article for our site, dealing with the possible course of ancient routes in Mariková and its surroundings. The subject of the presumed ancient road running below the Šimúnky hillfort is very popular today among those interested in our history, yet the article presented here is probably the first academically grounded text on the topic. We publish it in full. Our great thanks go to the author for such a sound text.
Peter Schreiber:
Šimúnky (Široká), Hradište, Koscelisko – possible connections

The subject of this article is the place names and archaeological sites of part of a microregion lying in the foothills and uplands of the Javorníky Mountains, and the possible relationship between them, with regard to the period of the Early Middle Ages.
Three places, three place names, which lie in the Mariková valley
and in the valley of the Biela voda stream
, represent remarkable landscape features. First of all, mention must be made of the unique archaeological site of Šimúnky (Široká)

. This place lies in the cadastral area of the village of Dolná Mariková (map 1). It is a hilltop settlement with evidence of occupation from various periods, from the Mesolithic or Neolithic, through the Púchov culture, to the medieval period (Májsky 2006; Malec 2010; Meliš 2003; Moravčík 2000). The nearest site with evidence of occupation also from the Early Middle Ages is Hatné, at the locality known as Hrádok (Moravčík 2002), c. 3.5 km from Šimúnky as the crow flies.

Below Šimúnky there is a smaller crossroads from which one can continue to Horná Mariková and on as far as the ridge of the Javorníky. From the point of view of the position of Šimúnky, however, the nearer route to Kátlina (a part of Dolná Mariková) may be more interesting. Forest tracks through Kátlina take us into the valley of the Biela voda. It is precisely here that two further sites lie which could theoretically also be connected with the occupation at Šimúnky.
These lie in the cadastral areas of the villages of Zbora

and Vydrná. The first is a site called Hradište (759 m above sea level). Hradište is interesting above all from the point of view of its name (as a toponym). So far nothing is known of any archaeological finds coming from this site

(map 1). In the surroundings of the hill, however, there are further remarkable names. In the village of Zbora there is a hamlet called Podhradište, and on the north-western slopes of Hradište there is the local name Hradište-Hrádza (map 1). In this context the older name of the Petríkovec stream should also be mentioned (map 1). Its lower course is given on older maps as Drahý potok. From the point of view of linguistics, similar places are explained as follows: “they are connected with the appellative drahá, which in Old Slovak denoted a road” (Uhlár 1970). Such a road (dráha) may be recorded precisely in the older name of this stream. The name of the Radotina stream should also be mentioned here (map 1). In part of the stem of this compound personal name the root Rad- is clearly present, which is frequent in the study of Slavic clan and personal names (Uhlár 1970, 110).

A further site, called Koscelisko, lies in the cadastral areas of the villages of Zbora/Mestečko (map 1). At the site there is a smaller rampart feature of oval shape. The name Koscelisko itself suggests the existence of occupation of an unspecified character. Names similar to Koscelisko can be associated with occupation of the medieval, or indeed the early medieval period.
Concluding thoughts:

The Mariková site of Šimúnky, with its striking archaeological finds from the Early Middle Ages, represents an important place within the wider region. For this reason, by studying the landscape, the place names and also the relief of the hills and the road communications, we have tried to identify the nearest places that could be directly
or indirectly
connected with the occupation at Šimúnky. The sites of Hradište and Koscelisko are among the nearest possible reference points in this research

. Both, like the Šimúnky site, lie in strongly dissected upland and mountainous terrain (Hrnčiarová 2002). Finally, I mention two further sites. The first is called Kňažová, in the cadastral area of the village of Lúky (map 1). Within this site of Kňažová there are smaller mound-like features. In interpreting them, however, a certain caution must for the time being be maintained, as they may be the remains of graves from abandoned fields. On the other hand, the local name Kňažia, which already appears on the Second Military Survey of Hungary (in the 19th century), might evoke a certain sacredness of this place in people's memory.
The second place is represented by the local name Jazerka. It lies c. 580 m north-east of the above-mentioned hamlet of Podhradište in Zbora
. The site is today under woodland, at the foot (on the slopes) of a mountain ridge
. In the case of this place, a water source, a small lake, could be deduced from the name alone

. Lakes or small lakes are precisely what pagan pre-Christian belief associated with religious veneration (Profantová/Profant 2004; 177, 178). The site of Jazerka may theoretically be just such a place, preserved in local tradition only as a name. The same significance in pagan belief, from prehistory to the medieval period (generally), was also held by unusual rock formations, for example isolated rocks in exposed places.
Acknowledgement: I would like to thank Stanislava Flimmelová for her cooperation and for valuable information.
